title: Saudi Strikes Houthi Port as Middle East Conflict Widens, Six Dead in West Bank Shooting, 220,000 Flee Europe's Wildfires
subhead: Saudi Arabia's military intervention against Houthi-held Hodeidah marks a dangerous widening of the Iran-US conflict's regional dimensions. Meanwhile, a deadly shooting in the occupied West Bank and catastrophic wildfires across France and Spain compound a day of escalating crises.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Strikes Houthi-Held Hodeidah
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia carried out military strikes against Houthi-held Hodeidah, Yemen's main Red Sea port, according to Houthi-controlled media. The Houthi Foreign Ministry warned the attack would trigger 'further escalation in the Yemeni conflict.' This marks a significant shift: Saudi Arabia had largely stayed out of the US-Iran confrontation, but the Houthi threat to Saudi oil tankers transiting the Red Sea — compounding the closure of Hormuz — appears to have drawn Riyadh back into direct military action against the Yemeni group.

The strike comes after the Houthis claimed attacks on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, threatening the Bab al-Mandab strait. With Hormuz closed, Saudi Arabia had been routing oil exports through its East-West Pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea. Houthi attacks on that route now threaten the kingdom's last viable export corridor. BBC reports crude oil has crossed back above $100 a barrel.

President Trump vowed 'major military punishment' against Iran for Houthi attacks and told Axios he was considering restarting major combat operations in Iran with strikes 'bigger than ever before.' The US and UK will hold a conference in London next week on the Strait of Hormuz, with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Dan Caine attending, according to the BBC.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia re-entering direct military action against the Houthis transforms a bilateral US-Iran confrontation into a broader regional war, and if both Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab are disrupted, global energy and trade flows face a two-chokepoint crisis.

sections.heading: Six Dead in Deadliest West Bank Incident in Months
sections.body:
At least four Palestinians and two Israelis were killed in a shooting in the village of Tal in the occupied West Bank — the deadliest single incident there in months. Conflicting accounts have emerged: Palestinians say settlers attacked homes and soldiers then shot residents, while the Israeli military says a Palestinian stole a security guard's weapon and killed him, with soldiers then killing the attacker and three members of his family.

The Israeli military said it is preparing 'extensive counterterrorism operational activity' in the area. Prime Minister Netanyahu and Defence Minister Katz issued a joint statement ordering the demolition of the Palestinian shooter's home and the acceleration of settlement outpost legalisation. Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said the villages of 'the murderers' must be treated 'the same way as Gaza.'

The US summoned Malaysia's envoy over Israel policy, and Trump said 'it's time' for Saudi Arabia to normalise ties with Israel — conditioning the US-Saudi nuclear deal on Riyadh joining the Abraham Accords. The incident further destabilises an already volatile West Bank, where the UN says 1,114 Palestinians and 41 Israelis have been killed since October 2023.
sections.whyItMatters: The West Bank is at its most dangerous point in years, with the Israeli government using a deadly incident to accelerate settlement expansion — a move that further erodes prospects for Palestinian statehood and fuels regional tensions at a moment when multiple Middle Eastern crises are converging.

sections.heading: Russia Kills 15 in Missile Strikes as Ukraine's Political Crisis Simmers
sections.body:
Russia killed at least 15 people in Ukraine on Friday, including 10 who died when three ballistic missiles struck a drone technology exhibition near Kyiv. The event was attended by prominent members of the Ukrainian defence sector. Air force spokesman Yuri Ihnat said only one of three missiles was intercepted. Russia's Defence Ministry confirmed the attack, claiming it targeted 'producers of drones' and representatives involved in 'strikes on Russian territory.'

The strike drew outrage over why a widely advertised public event was held during wartime. President Zelensky said the incident was being investigated, and the prosecutor-general is examining who authorised the event and what safety measures were in place.

Meanwhile, Zelensky's political crisis over his removal of Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov continues to reverberate. Fedorv rejected Zelensky's offers of alternative posts, saying only the defence ministry, the military chief role, or the presidency were 'worth having.' His reference to the presidency was widely noted as a potential challenge to Zelensky. The appointment of respected Maj Gen Mykhailo Drapatyi as commander-in-chief has only partially resolved the crisis. Zelensky is expected to meet Trump in Washington on Tuesday.
sections.whyItMatters: The missile strike on a public exhibition reveals a dangerous gap in Ukraine's operational security, while the Fedorov crisis is draining political energy at a critical moment — Ukraine needs unity before what Zelensky warned could be another major Russian assault within 48 hours.

sections.heading: ICC Removes Prosecutor Karim Khan as Institution Faces Dual Threats
sections.body:
The International Criminal Court's 125 member states voted 82 to remove chief prosecutor Karim Khan over sexual misconduct allegations. Khan, a British lawyer elected in 2021, was found by the court's oversight body to have committed 'serious breach of duty and serious misconduct' by engaging in an improper relationship with a junior staff member and trying to stop her complaint. Khan denies the allegations and his lawyer said he would challenge the decision.

The removal coincides with an unprecedented US campaign to dismantle the ICC. The Trump administration has launched a 'whole-of-government' effort to take the court apart 'brick by brick,' imposing visa bans, asset freezes, and diplomatic pressure on allies to withdraw. Khan himself was barred from entering the US under Trump administration sanctions over the ICC's investigation into alleged Israeli war crimes in Gaza.

Venezuela separately announced it would withdraw from the ICC, accusing it of 'bias' — a move that aligns with the Trump administration's anti-ICC stance. The EU also announced new sanctions on Russia, including on FIDE chess president Arkady Dvorkovich, a former Russian deputy prime minister.
sections.whyItMatters: The ICC faces a pincer movement: internal scandal weakens its legitimacy precisely as the United States mounts the most serious external challenge in the court's history. Khan's removal may be justified on the merits, but it hands ammunition to those who want the institution dismantled entirely.

sections.heading: Trump Hits EU With Tech Investigation and 60-Nation Tariff Wave
sections.body:
President Trump announced a Section 301 investigation into the European Union over its regulation of American tech companies, threatening a 'substantial tariff' in response to fines levied against Google, Apple, Meta, and Amazon. The move came days after the European Commission fined Google €890m for squeezing out competitors under the Digital Markets Act. Trump claimed Apple had been fined $15bn, Meta $3bn, and Amazon $2.5bn by the EU — figures whose provenance was unclear.

Simultaneously, the US imposed new 10-12.5% tariffs on 60 trading partners covering 99.4% of American imports, replacing an identical temporary levy that expired Friday. The tariffs are nominally justified by forced labour concerns, but trade expert Caroline Freund of UC San Diego told the BBC that Trump was 'looking for a legal reason to put the tariffs in' and that the real motivation is reducing trade deficits and boosting US manufacturing.

The UK's Chambers of Commerce said Britain had lost its comparative advantage against the EU, which secured a flat 10% deal. Brazil called its 12.5% rate 'unjustified,' Japan 'regretted' the move, and Australia's trade minister called it 'completely unjustified.' China denied forced labour exists and accused Washington of 'political manipulation.' Two US small businesses have already filed suit challenging the tariffs' legal basis.
sections.whyItMatters: The dual moves — tech investigation and tariff renewal — represent a systematic escalation of Trump's economic confrontation with allies and rivals alike, risking a further fracturing of global trade relationships at a moment when supply chains are already strained by the Middle East crisis.

sections.heading: Catastrophic Wildfires Force 220,000 From Homes in France and Spain
sections.body:
More than 220,000 people have been evacuated from wildfires raging across south-west France and central Spain in what officials are calling some of the worst fires in both countries' histories. In France, around 200,000 people have been evacuated from the Gironde and Landes regions, with four towns near Bordeaux — including Saint-Médard-en-Jalles, with 58,400 residents — ordered to clear out overnight. The Gironde fire, described by local prefect Sophie Brocas as an 'XXL fire,' has burned through more than 19,000 hectares and destroyed about 80 homes. France's interior minister said the blaze was 'self-sustaining' and moving toward Bordeaux.

In Spain, three fires west of Madrid merged into a single blaze that regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso called 'the worst fire in the history of the region.' More than 60,000 people have been affected — 25,000 evacuated, nearly 40,000 told to stay indoors. Firefighters said the blaze was 'beyond the capacity' of crews to contain. The EU has deployed aircraft and helicopters to support both countries, and France activated the EU's civil protection mechanism, receiving Black Hawk helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

The European Forest Fire Information System reports that wildfires have already burned more land in Europe this year than the annual average for the past two decades. Europe is warming at more than twice the global average, according to the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service.
sections.whyItMatters: The scale of simultaneous evacuations across two major European nations is unprecedented, and the fire season is far from over. With Hormuz disrupted and global energy logistics already strained, a sustained climate emergency in southern Europe will compound economic pressure and test EU solidarity.

bottomLine: Saudi Arabia's decision to strike Houthi-held Hodeidah marks a qualitative escalation that draws Riyadh back into direct military engagement in Yemen — and transforms the Iran-US confrontation from a two-party conflict into a regional one. If both Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab remain disrupted, the global economy faces a two-chokepoint supply crisis with oil above $100. On the ground in Israel-Palestine, the West Bank shooting and Israel's subsequent settlement acceleration further erode prospects for stability. The ICC's removal of Karim Khan weakens the court at the exact moment the Trump administration is trying to dismantle it. And 220,000 people fleeing wildfires in France and Spain is a climate-driven emergency compounding an already strained European summer.
